## `dplyr`

- `base R` functions and operators are what we have been working with thus far. "base" refers to the core set of software (e.g., functions) that comes when you initially download R. We can extend the power of R through downloading different *R packages*. `dplyr` is an `R package` which contains a variety of consistently-structured functions for `data wrangling`.

-   *Package*: A collection of functions, data sets, and other code that is bundled together for a specific purpose that follows a specific theme. It extends the functionality of the base R software that comes with the initial download of R. One example is the `terra` package, which contains functions to help you work with spatial data.

-   *Data wrangling*: Data wrangling is the process of transforming data from its raw form into another form with the specific intent to make it more valuable and usable for downstream purposes including visualization and statistical analysis. `dplyr` is an R package that has the purpose to extend R's functionality for data wrangling and visualization.

Using the dplyr package requires introducing the concept of installing and loading packages in R. Everything you have done in R prior to this can be done with the base R software that comes with the initial download of R. But if you want to extend what you can do with R, you will need to install new packages that contain new functionality. All you need is the name of the package you want to install, and then you can pass that name as a *character* into the `install.packages()` function. Installing the dplyr package would look like this: install.packages("dplyr"). No need to do this here, it has already been done for you; we will revisit this in the near future.

### Important

-   *You only need to install an R package once*.
-   *But, with each new R session, you must load the package*. This is achieved using the `library()` function, where you just pass in the name of the installed package into the function. Since the tidyverse package has already been installed for you, you can load the tidyverse package with the code below:

```{r demo_load, exercise = TRUE}

#load the dplyr package
library(dplyr)

```

### Tidy Basics Refresher

Data wrangling is built around the idea of organizing data tables according to "tidy" data principles:

-   Every variable is a column
-   Every observation is a row
-   Every value is a cell

This tutorial is focused on key data wrangling functions that originate from a package called "dplyr" (a riff on "data pliers"). 

**pro tip:** *The first argument in all of these tidyverse functions is the name of the data frame*.

## A note on positional arguments

Up to this tutorial, you have been very explicit in defining the name of the arguments passed into the functions you have been using; these are called `named arguments`. For example:

```{r demo_argument_1, exercise = TRUE}

#named arguments example with iris and head() function
head(x = iris, n = 2)

```

The above is an example of using named arguments by clearly linking the "x" argument (an object) to the iris data frame and the "n" argument (an integer vector) to the number of rows to preview.

R also can also do `positional arguments` to circumvent naming every argument. R can infer what the argument is based on the *position* of the value being passed into the function. This is common practice in frequently used functions. For example:

```{r demo_argument_2, exercise = TRUE}

#positional arguments example with iris and head() function
head(iris, 2)

```

The above is an example of using an example of positional arguments. R understands what each argument is based off its position because in the `head()` function the name of the object always comes *first* while the number of rows to preview always comes *second*.

The key dplyr functions take advantage of R's ability to use positional arguments.

## The `mutate()` function

The `mutate()` function calculates or adds a new variable to a data frame, **resulting in a new column**. The typical result is the addition of a column. The first (positional) argument passed into the function is the *name of the data frame*. The second argument specifies the *new variable*, including the name *and* the value. For example, if you wanted to create and add a new variable to the iris data frame called "ratio" that is calculated as Sepal.Width divided by Sepal.Length, it would look as such:

```{r demo_mutate, exercise = TRUE}

#create a new variable named ratio using mutate:
iris <- mutate(iris, ratio = Sepal.Width/Sepal.Length)
head(iris, 1)

```

The second argument in the `mutate()` function is an example of a "name-value" pair; to the left of `=` is the name of the *new variable* while to the right of `=` is the value and/or calculation associated with it. Notice how the calculation above used existing variables.

The analog using an extraction operator would be:

```{r demo_mutate_2, exercise = TRUE}

#create a new variable named ratio using an extraction operator
iris$ratio <- iris$Sepal.Width/iris$Sepal.Length
head(iris, 1)
```

The two code chunks above do the same thing and work in the same way. *Remember that variables (columns) in a data frame are just atomic vectors*. Both approaches above are just dividing two vectors of the same length by each other to generate a new atomic vector which, in this case, produces a new variable/column in the iris data frame called "ratio".

## The `filter()` function

The `filter()` function excludes (subsets) data according to a set criteria that is specified using a `comparison operator`. The typical result is a reduction in the number of rows. The first argument is the name of the data frame, the second argument is the condition. As one example, you may only be interested in analyzing one species in a data frame that contains data for multiple species. If you wanted to filter the iris data frame to include only rows with the setosa species, it would look as such:

```{r demo_filter_1, exercise = TRUE}

#filter iris data frame to rows with data only for setosa using filter function
setosa_tidy <- filter(iris, Species == "setosa")
head(setosa_tidy, 5)
```

The analog using extraction operators would be:

```{r demo_filter_2, exercise = TRUE}

#filter iris data frame to rows with data only for setosa using extraction operator
setosa_extraction <- iris[iris$Species == "setosa",]
head(setosa_extraction, 5)

```

## The `select()` function

The `select()` function selects a specific column(s) from a data frame. The typical result is a reduction in the number of columns. The first argument of the function is the name of the data frame, while the second argument is the name (or a vector of names) of the column. There is no need for placing column names in quotations here or even using `c()` to define a sequence of multiple columns. If you wanted to select the Petal.Width column from the iris data frame, it would look as such:

```{r demo_select_1, exercise = TRUE}

#select Petal.Width column using the select function
petal_width_tidy <- select(iris, Petal.Width)
head(petal_width_tidy, 5)

```

The analog using an extraction operator would be:

```{r demo_select_2, exercise = TRUE}

#select Petal.Width using an extraction operator
petal_width_extraction <- iris$Petal.Width
head(petal_width_extraction, 5)

#could also do this:
petal_width_extraction_2 <- iris[,"Petal.Width"]
head(petal_width_extraction_2, 5)

```

Note how the dplyr version returns a data frame, while the extraction operator version returns an atomic vector. There are workarounds using operators, but the implicit expectation from dplyr is that you'd like to continue working in a data frame, which is usually the case.

## The `arrange()` function

Finally, the `select()` function orders rows in a data frame according to ascending or descending values in a variable. The typical result is a reordering of rows. The first argument is the name of the data frame while the second argument is the variable to arrange *all* rows by. The default is ascending but you can specify if you want the order to be descending. For example, if you wanted to order rows in the iris data frame according to *ascending* values of Petal.Length, it would look as such:

```{r demo_arrange_1, exercise = TRUE}

#arrange rows in the iris data frame by low to high values of Petal.Length
petal_length_low_high <- arrange(iris, Petal.Length)
head(petal_length_low_high, 5)

```

If you wanted to order rows according to *descending* values (high to low) of Petal.Length, you need to specify this using a nested `desc()` function, which you can nest within the `arrange()` function:

```{r demo_arrange_2, exercise = TRUE}

#arrange rows in the iris data frame by high to low values of Petal.Length
petal_length_high_low <- arrange(iris, desc(Petal.Length))
head(petal_length_high_low, 5)

```

## Problem Set

### Q1: Mutate it

First, use the `mutate()` function to calculate and add a new variable (column) to the iris data frame called Petal.Area that is calculated by multiplying Petal.Width by Petal.Length. Make ssure that this new variable gets stored in the iris data frame as a column.

```{r problem_1, exercise=TRUE}


```

```{r problem_1-hint}

Use the assignment operator to ensure this new variable gets stored in iris

```

```{r problem_1-solution}

iris <- mutate(iris, Petal.Area = Petal.Length*Petal.Width)

```

```{r problem_1-check}
grade_code()
```

### Q2: Filter it

Second, use the `filter()` function to filter to rows that are above the *average* value of Petal.Area and assign this new filtered data frame the name "iris_filtered".

```{r problem_2,exercise = TRUE, exercise.setup = "problem_1-solution"}


```

```{r problem_2-hint}

What function calculates an average?

```

```{r problem_2-solution}

iris_filtered <- filter(iris, Petal.Area > mean(Petal.Area))

```

```{r problem_2-check}

grade_code()

```

### Q3: Select it

```{r problem_3_setup,include=FALSE}

iris <- mutate(iris, Petal.Area = Petal.Length*Petal.Width)
iris_filtered <- filter(iris, Petal.Area > mean(Petal.Area))

```

Third, use the `select()` function to return a data frame with only the Species and Petal.Area columns, using the "iris_filtered" data frame you created.

```{r problem_3,exercise = TRUE,exercise.setup = "problem_3_setup"}



```

```{r problem_3-hint}

No need to use a nested `c()` function here!

```

```{r problem_3-solution}

select(iris_filtered, Species, Petal.Area)

```

```{r problem_3-check}

grade_code()

```

### Q4: Arrange it

```{r problem_4_setup,include=FALSE}

iris <- mutate(iris, Petal.Area = Petal.Length*Petal.Width)
iris_filtered <- filter(iris, Petal.Area > mean(Petal.Area))

```

Finally, use the `arrange()` function to order the rows of the "iris_filtered" dataframe by descending value of Petal.Area.

```{r problem_4,exercise = TRUE,exercise.setup = "problem_4_setup"}


```

```{r problem_4-hint}

Use a nested `desc()` function!

```

```{r problem_4-solution}

arrange(iris_filtered, desc(Petal.Area))

```

```{r problem_4-check}
grade_code()
```
